newsitem.title: USA: Second Okla. City bomb suspect seeks separate trial.
newsitem.headline: Second Okla. City bomb suspect seeks separate trial.

text.p: Attorneys for Oklahoma City bombing suspect Terry Nichols on Friday asked that his trial be separated from co-defendant Timothy McVeigh, saying the evidence against McVeigh is much stronger.

"The cases against Mr. McVeigh and Mr. Nichols differ dramatically in every relevant respect; the quantity and quality of the evidence against each; the degree of culpability for the crime demonstrated and the character of each defendant for sentencing purposes," Nichols' attorneys wrote in a filing with the court.
Earlier this week, McVeigh also asked for a separate trial. U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch will hold a hearing on the matter on Oct. 2.
Matsch will then set a trial date, which is expected either late this year or early next year. The trial has been moved to Denver from Oklahoma City to try to ensure a fair trail.
Nichols' attorneys also asked for a separate penalty phase if the two men are tried together and found guilty.

"The undisputed fact that Mr. Nichols was not at the scene of the crime and had no participation in the actual placement and detonation of the bomb ... also means that there is substantial room for residual doubt as well as reasonable doubt about his intentions, even if the jury convicts him of a capital crime," the lawyers said.
Prosecutors, who are seeking the death penalty, want to try the men together. Nichols' attorneys said that because the penalty could be death the court should take extra care to separate the trials.
The two defendants are charged with the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building which killed 168 people.

Nichols' attorneys argued that separate trials should be granted because highly prejudicial evidence that will not be admissible against their client is likely to be admitted against McVeigh and would produce a "near-certainty of prejudicial confusion."
McVeigh is seeking a separate trial because of statements Nichols made about McVeigh that could be devastating to McVeigh, his attorneys argued in their brief.
